I like Dex, but his analogy here almost feels intentionally ignorant of the situation here.

"If public e-bike company gave you a subscription on rides and you proceeded to around ripping out batteries and sticking them in your own bike and ride around town, you’d get banned for that too. Especially if your bike was poorly wired and overloaded the batteries/cause them to flame up etc."

Let's fix the analogy.

First, we need to separate the "e-bike" and the "battery". The bikes are a commodity. You can download 10 options for free on GitHub. You just have to bring your own battery.

Now we have lots of bikes and a shortage of batteries. Only two companies make batteries. Well, there's actually like 10, but 8 of them are less reliable and only hold 1/4th the charge. One of them makes your bike drive off the road sometimes. So we're stuck with two real options.

The batteries are EXPENSIVE. Like $100 each. (assume they're single-use for this to work, again this is the bullshit Dex gave me to work with here). Some people only use $10 of charge a month. Others user $100 a week. We all pay roughly the same rate when we need new batteries.

Then suddenly, one of the two battery companies offers a new plan - $200/month, but you get up to $5,000 in battery replacements. HOORAH!

But there's a catch - you can only use the batteries in THEIR bikes. Wait, what? There's so many options! Sucks for you, they want you to use THEIR bikes. Btw, you can't actually modify them or fix them when they break. And they break. A LOT. Constantly even. And they hide all the details of how they're built.

Your friend next door has a bike from GitHub. It works great. He has no issues. The schematics are public. He can fix it however he want. He can even use Anthropic's batteries! He just has to pay full price.

You get a massive discount, you just have to deal with a shitty, opaque, unreliable, slow, fucked up bike.

recent_posts.title: GitHub alternatives compared from GitLab to Forgejo and next-gen options
recent_posts.summary: A deep-dive comparison of GitHub alternatives as developers consider leaving due to reliability issues. GitLab is criticized for poor UX and massive codebase complexity. Bitbucket is dismissed as primarily a cost-saving tool for Atlassian shops. Forgejo and Codeberg emerge as the recommended open-source self-hostable options, praised for clean Go codebase, solid release tooling, and nonprofit governance. Pierre's code.sto is highlighted as a next-generation Git infrastructure built for high-throughput agentic workflows. Graphite (acquired by Cursor) and Entire (founded by GitHub's ex-CEO) are flagged as potential Gen 3 players. The piece ends with a lament about the fragmentation of GitHub's developer community, arguing that no tool can replace the social graph that GitHub built over 20 years.
